extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates / graduate students and researchers in enumerative combinatorics and algebraic combinatorics
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and methods to represent and compute multivariate generating functions E(x) for nonnegative integer (N-)solutions to linear homogeneous Diophantine systems, including geometric (cone/triangulation) decompositions, simplicial monoids, rationality and reciprocity theorems, and applications (e.g., counting magic squares).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: quasipolynomial
rubrics_metrics.description: A quasipolynomial of degree d is a function f : N → C of the form f(n) = cd(n) n^d + cd-1(n) n^{d-1} + ... + c0(n), where each ci(n) is a periodic function (with integer period) and cd(n) is not identically zero; equivalently there exists an integer N>0 (a quasiperiod) and polynomials f0,...,f_{N-1} such that f(n)=f_i(n) when n ≡ i (mod N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The integer N is not unique; any common period of the coefficient functions works and is called a quasiperiod. This is the working definition used to recognize/quasi-polynomial behavior of counting functions arising from rational generating functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent characterizations of quasipolynomials (Proposition 4.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : N → C and an integer N>0 the following are equivalent: (i) f is a quasipolynomial of quasiperiod N; (ii) the ordinary generating function ∑_{n≥0} f(n) x^n equals P(x)/Q(x) with P,Q ∈ C[x], deg P < deg Q, and every zero α of Q(x) satisfies α^N = 1 (after reduction to lowest terms); (iii) for all n≥0, f(n) = ∑_{i=1}^k P_i(n) γ_i^n where each P_i is a polynomial and each γ_i satisfies γ_i^N = 1. Moreover, deg P_i equals one less than multiplicity of γ_i^{-1} as a root of Q(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives practical checks: rational generating function with denominator roots roots of unity implies quasipolynomiality and predicts the exponentials and polynomial factors contributing to the explicit form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falling-factorial basis and discrete Taylor expansion / coefficients from difference table
rubrics_metrics.description: Polynomials (n choose i) for i=0..d form a basis for P_d, and when a polynomial f(n) is expanded in this basis the coefficients are given by the forward differences: f(n) = ∑_{i=0}^d (Δ^i f(0)) (n choose i) (discrete analogue of Taylor series). Equivalently, the coefficients in the expansion are the elements of the diagonal of the difference table beginning with f(0) and moving southwest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a canonical way to expand integer-indexed polynomials and read off coefficients via finite differences; transition matrices between bases involve Stirling numbers (first and second kind). Example given: f(n)=n^3+n+1 expansion and its difference table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition matrices between bases (monomials and falling/rising factorials)
rubrics_metrics.description: By Proposition 1.9.2 the transition matrices between the bases n^i and (n)_i (falling factorial) are essentially the Stirling numbers of the first and second kinds: (n)^j = ∑_i s(j,i) (n)_i and (n)_i = ∑_j S(j,i) (n)^j, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these relations to convert expansions given in one basis to another; important when relating ordinary polynomial bases to combinatorial factorial bases for generating-function manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model: solutions to Φ α = 0 form a monoid E and associated multivariate generating function E(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an r×m integer matrix Φ, the set of N-solutions E = { α ∈ N^m : Φ α = 0 } is a (commutative) monoid; its multivariate generating function is E(x) = ∑_{α∈E} x^α where x^α = x_1^{α1}···x_m^{αm}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to understand algebraic/geometric structure of E (as a union of simplicial monoids) and to derive rationality and structural properties of E(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose E via polyhedral cone triangulation into simplicial monoids (Lemma 4.5.1–4.5.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: View the real cone C of nonnegative real solutions to Φ α = 0; it is a pointed convex polyhedral cone with finitely many extreme rays. There exists a triangulation Γ of C into simplicial cones σ such that E = ⋃_{σ ∈ Γ} E_σ where E_σ = σ ∩ N^m is a simplicial submonoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This geometric decomposition is the basis for expressing E(x) as a combination of simpler generating functions E_σ(x). One must handle overlaps (intersections) of the simplicial parts via Möbius inversion on the face lattice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Möbius-inversion relations for generating functions (Lemma 4.5.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a triangulation Γ of C into simplicial cones, the multivariate generating functions satisfy E(x) = ∑_{σ∈Γ} μ(σ,ˆ1) E_σ(x) and E(x) = ∑_{σ∈Γ^∘} E_σ(x), where μ is the Möbius function of the face poset of the triangulation and Γ^∘ denotes interior facets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute E(x) by combining the rational generating functions of the simplicial submonoids E_σ with Möbius coefficients to correct for overlaps; the second formula gives a disjoint-union decomposition for the interior part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generating function of a simplicial monoid (Corollary 4.5.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F ⊆ N^m is a simplicial monoid with quasigenerators α1,...,α_t and finite sets D_F (resp. D^F) of coset representatives, then F(x) = (∑_{β∈D_F} x^β) / ∏_{i=1}^t (1 - x^{α_i}) and F^∘(x) = (∑_{β∈D^F} x^β) / ∏_{i=1}^t (1 - x^{α_i}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an explicit rational form for each simplicial piece: a finite numerator (sum over a fundamental parallelepiped / coset representatives) and a product denominator encoding the quasigenerators; choose quasigenerators consistently to compute the finite numerator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completely fundamental elements CF(E) and denominator structure (Proposition 4.5.10 & Theorem 4.5.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set CF(E) of completely fundamental elements of E can be described equivalently as: (i) the completely fundamental elements; (ii) ⋃_{σ∈Γ} CF(E_σ); (iii) nonzero elements β ∈ E that lie on an extreme ray of C and are not proper integer multiples of any other element in E; (iv) minimal-support non-divisible elements. Theorem 4.5.11: E(x) and E^∘(x) are rational functions and, when reduced to lowest terms, both have denominator D(x) = ∏_{β∈CF(E)} (1 - x^β).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To write E(x) in lowest terms, identify CF(E): these elements determine the irreducible cyclotomic factors in the denominator (as monomial factors 1-x^β). The theorem includes a uniqueness argument (irreducibility of monomials x^γ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity theorem for simplicial monoids and for general monoid E (Lemmas 4.5.12–4.5.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F ⊆ N^m is a simplicial monoid of dimension t then F(x) = (-1)^t F(1/x). More generally, for the monoid E of N-solutions to Φ α = 0 which is positive and with d = dim C, E^∘(x) = (-1)^d E(1/x) (reciprocity theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combinatorial/geometric reciprocity: for simplicial pieces the finite numerator/denominator expression yields the sign change on substitution x→1/x; combine via Möbius inversion and gradedness of face lattice to get the full reciprocity. Reciprocity can be used to derive symmetry and sign relations for specialized counting functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization and univariate counting generating function (Lemma 4.5.17)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given linear functional L(α)=a_1 α_1 + ... + a_m α_m with finite level sets in E and corresponding counting sequence g(r)=# {α∈E : L(α)=r} (assumed g(r)>0 for some r>0), the univariate generating function G(λ)=∑_{r≥0} g(r) λ^r equals the multivariate specialization E(λ^{a_1},...,λ^{a_m}) (notation in text: E(λ a_1, ..., λ a_m)) and G is a rational function with negative degree (deg G(λ) < 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This specialization principle reduces multivariate rationality to univariate rational generating functions for counting problems (e.g., sums of coordinates, magic-square row/column sums) and is used to deduce polynomial/quasipolynomial behavior of g(r).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application: magic squares — CF(E) are permutation matrices and H_n(r) is a polynomial
rubrics_metrics.description: For the monoid E of n×n nonnegative integer matrices with all row and column sums equal to r, CF(E) consists exactly of the n! permutation matrices. Consequently the specialized counting function H_n(r) (number of such matrices) is a polynomial in r of degree (n-1)^2; it vanishes at r = -1, -2, ..., -(n-1) and satisfies a reciprocity relation derived from E(1/x) = ± x^γ E(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses identification of completely fundamental elements with permutation matrices (minimal-support non-divisible elements) and applies Theorem 4.5.11 and specialization lemma to deduce polynomiality and symmetry properties; concrete computation of H_n(r) can be done by determining finitely many values (degree bounds give how many) and using vanishing/reciprocity relations.
